doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: Why transposed parts matter and the Locrian device
summary: A story of concert-key Giant Steps; Tiberi refuses concert parts and explains practicing the dominant instead of minor seven flat five.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. You just gave me a flash. I attended an improv workshop after I graduated from college and this fella’s approach was this was in a roomful of improvisers. Some people had never even done it. And he passed out “Giant Steps” in the concert key and he expected everybody to play it. And the results were not pretty, I can tell you that.

Never. I know that. I know that even just last week I had a student that wanted to play a tune and he said he had the tune but the back tracking was on his iPhone you know. And all the back tracks that I do actually are pretty much with strings and everything and all that, a little more encouragement. And he had a concert part. And I says, “Noah,” I says, “I’m not going to play a concert because I don’t like it.” You know I wouldn’t be able to perform exactly what I know. I’d have to transpose it first and then I’ve got to remember some of the concept things that I teach. I can’t do it. I mean you know you know if you see a C chord maybe you know it’s a D. But I mean if you go like a minor seven flat five then, or a major seven flat five or something like that — and then of course there are devices that I use for them incidentally. In other words you don’t practice on a minor seven flat five. It’s a Locrian.
So you practice on the dominant. You don’t practice on the major seven flat five because I mean one tone higher it’s a dominant.
I see. Well if we ever do a gig together I’m going to remember to being transposed parts for you.

Right. But I do, I mean it’s a lot of effort but I enjoy doing it actually so this way they’re able to really — and everybody, most of the piano players or most of the teachers do give out the concert parts and I don’t — it holds back, it really does.
